questions.stem: The reaction sequence(s) that would lead to o-xylene as the major product is(are)

options.text: Starting compound (shown): 1. NaNO₂/HCl, 273 K; 2. CuCN; 3. DIBAL-H then H₃O⁺; 4. N₂H₄, KOH, heat
Starting compound (shown): 1. Mg, CO₂, H₃O⁺; 2. SOCl₂; 3. H₂, Pd-BaSO₄; 4. Zn-Hg, HCl
Starting compound (shown): 1. i. BH₃ ii. H₂O₂, NaOH; 2. PBr₃; 3. Zn, dil. HCl
Starting compound (shown): 1. O₃, Zn/H₂O; 2. N₂H₄, KOH, heat

questions.solution: (A) o-Toluidine → diazonium salt → o-tolunitrile (Sandmeyer) → o-tolualdehyde (DIBAL-H) → o-xylene (Wolff–Kishner). (B) 2-Bromotoluene → Grignard + CO₂ → o-toluic acid → acid chloride → aldehyde (Rosenmund) → o-xylene (Clemmensen). (C) Anti-Markovnikov hydroboration puts the OH on the terminal carbon. After bromination and reduction the product is 2-ethyltoluene. (D) Ozonolysis of indene gives (2-formylphenyl)acetaldehyde, and Wolff–Kishner reduction then gives 2-ethyltoluene. So only A and B lead to o-xylene.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; the official key is not in the archived paper

questions.stem:
Correct option(s) for the following sequence of reactions is(are)
PhCH₃ —Br₂, light→ P —1. Q; 2. H₂, Pd/C→ R —CHCl₃, KOH→ S (foul smelling)
P —V→ S
PhCH₃ —i. KMnO₄, KOH, heat; ii. H₃O⁺→ T —1. NH₃; 2. heat→ U —W→ R
questions.solution: P is benzyl bromide. AgNO₂ (attack through N) gives phenylnitromethane, and hydrogenation of that gives benzylamine R (phenylmethanamine). KNO₂ would mainly give the nitrite ester instead. In the carbylamine reaction R gives benzyl isocyanide S, the foul-smelling product. S can also be made from P in one step with AgCN, so V = AgCN (KCN gives the nitrile). On the other route, T is benzoic acid and U is benzamide, and LiAlH₄ reduces benzamide to benzylamine, so W = LiAlH₄.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; the official key is not in the archived paper

questions.stem:
Reaction of x g of Sn with HCl quantitatively produced a salt. Entire amount of the salt reacted with y g of nitrobenzene in the presence of required amount of HCl to produce 1.29 g of an organic salt (quantitatively).
(Use Molar masses (in g mol⁻¹) of H, C, N, O, Cl and Sn as 1, 12, 14, 16, 35 and 119, respectively).
The value of x is ___.
questions.solution: Sn + 2HCl → SnCl₂ + H₂. Reducing nitrobenzene to anilinium chloride is a 6-electron change: C₆H₅NO₂ + 3SnCl₂ + 7HCl → C₆H₅NH₃⁺Cl⁻ + 3SnCl₄ + 2H₂O. The organic salt C₆H₈NCl has M = 129 g mol⁻¹, so 1.29 g = 0.010 mol. That needs 0.030 mol SnCl₂, i.e. 0.030 mol Sn = 0.030 × 119 = 3.57 g.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; the official key is not in the archived paper

questions.stem:
Reaction of x g of Sn with HCl quantitatively produced a salt. Entire amount of the salt reacted with y g of nitrobenzene in the presence of required amount of HCl to produce 1.29 g of an organic salt (quantitatively).
(Use Molar masses (in g mol⁻¹) of H, C, N, O, Cl and Sn as 1, 12, 14, 16, 35 and 119, respectively).
The value of y is ___.
questions.solution: The salt is anilinium chloride, C₆H₅NH₃⁺Cl⁻ (129 g mol⁻¹), so 1.29 g corresponds to 0.010 mol. Each nitrobenzene gives one anilinium ion, so 0.010 mol C₆H₅NO₂ (123 g mol⁻¹) was used. y = 0.010 × 123 = 1.23 g.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; the official key is not in the archived paper

questions.passage:
The amount of energy required to break a bond is same as the amount of energy released when the same bond is formed. In gaseous state, the energy required for homolytic cleavage of a bond is called Bond Dissociation Energy (BDE) or Bond Strength. BDE is affected by s-character of the bond and the stability of the radicals formed. Shorter bonds are typically stronger bonds. BDEs for some bonds are given below:
H₃C–H(g) → H₃C•(g) + H•(g)   ΔH° = 105 kcal mol⁻¹
Cl–Cl(g) → Cl•(g) + Cl•(g)   ΔH° = 58 kcal mol⁻¹
H₃C–Cl(g) → H₃C•(g) + Cl•(g)   ΔH° = 85 kcal mol⁻¹
H–Cl(g) → H•(g) + Cl•(g)   ΔH° = 103 kcal mol⁻¹
questions.stem:
Correct match of the C–H bonds (shown in bold) in Column J with their BDE in Column K is
Column J (Molecule): (P) H–CH(CH₃)₂; (Q) H–CH₂Ph; (R) H–CH=CH₂; (S) H–C≡CH
Column K (BDE, kcal mol⁻¹): (i) 132; (ii) 110; (iii) 95; (iv) 88

options.text: P – iii, Q – iv, R – ii, S – i
P – i, Q – ii, R – iii, S – iv
P – iii, Q – ii, R – i, S – iv
P – ii, Q – i, R – iv, S – iii

questions.solution: A C–H bond is weaker when the radical formed is more stable, and stronger when the carbon has more s-character. The benzylic radical is resonance-stabilised, so H–CH₂Ph is the weakest (88). The tertiary isopropyl C–H, on sp³ carbon, comes next (95). The vinylic sp² C–H is stronger (110), and the alkynyl sp C–H is strongest (132). So P–iii, Q–iv, R–ii, S–i.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; the official key is not in the archived paper

questions.stem:
For the following reaction
CH₄(g) + Cl₂(g) —light→ CH₃Cl(g) + HCl(g)
the correct statement is

options.text: Initiation step is exothermic with ΔH° = −58 kcal mol⁻¹.
Propagation step involving •CH₃ formation is exothermic with ΔH° = −2 kcal mol⁻¹.
Propagation step involving CH₃Cl formation is endothermic with ΔH° = +27 kcal mol⁻¹.
The reaction is exothermic with ΔH° = −25 kcal mol⁻¹.

questions.solution: Initiation, Cl₂ → 2Cl•, only breaks a bond: ΔH = +58 (endothermic). CH₄ + Cl• → •CH₃ + HCl: ΔH = 105 − 103 = +2 (endothermic). •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl•: ΔH = 58 − 85 = −27 (exothermic). Overall: 105 + 58 − 85 − 103 = −25 kcal mol⁻¹, so only D is correct.

check.note: Two independent solutions agree; the official key is not in the archived paper
